title: Same tree
label: idb-list
statement: Given two binary trees, say whether they are **the same**: identical shape, with equal values in matching positions.
provenance: **InterviewDB-listed.** LeetCode 100 is on the LinkedIn list you supplied from InterviewDB. No candidate report of this exact question was found in the research passes — the evidence is that the list names it. On that list it uses the same pattern as InterviewDB Q17. The lockstep two-tree recursion that Q17 is built on. Same Tree returns a bool at the point where Q17 returns a merged node, and it is worth writing once to see that the shape is identical.

stages.title: Same shape, same values
stages.say: Say whether two binary trees are identical.
stages.require: Implement `SameTree.Check(p, q)`. Two empty trees are the same. Must not overflow on a tree 100,000 levels deep.

listen: Restates the problem and asks the clarifying questions that change the code (Are two empty trees the same? (Yes.); How deep can the trees get? (Assume very deep — a recursive solution c)
States the data structure, the invariant and the complexity before prompting
Reads AI output before running it

1.a: No — [1,2] (left child) and [1,null,2] (right child) have the same in-order with null markers removed.

2.a: O(n) time; O(h) memory for the stack.
Recursive is clearer; iterative survives a 100,000-deep chain. Say which you chose and why.

4.a: Store a Merkle hash per node (hash of value + children hashes); equal roots are equal trees in O(1).

5.a: Subtree of another tree (LeetCode 572) — the same hash idea finds it in O(n).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Given two binary trees, say whether they are **the same**: identical shape, with equal values in matching positions.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Are two empty trees the same? (Yes.)
- How deep can the trees get? (Assume very deep — a recursive solution can overflow the stack.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Walk both trees in lock-step, comparing node pairs. The recursive version is three lines; an explicit stack does the same thing without risking a stack overflow on a skewed tree.

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Make the design decision yourself, then ask the assistant to attack it.
- Delegate the mechanical parts only after the structure is fixed.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe compare node pairs in lock-step — both null is equal, one null or different values is not — with an explicit stack so depth cannot overflow: O(n). Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Check concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Comparing only the values in an in-order walk — different shapes can give the same sequence.
- Not handling the "one null, one not" case before reading `.Value`.
- Deep recursion on a skewed tree.
